list.listitem: In patients with chronic pruritus (≥6 weeks), consider checking CBC, ferritin, ESR, CRP, glucose, serum creatinine, LFTs, TSH, LDH, and stool occult blood (for age ≥40). C
First-line treatment is with an H1-receptor blocker. B
Second-line and adjunctive treatment options include H2-receptor blockers, montelukast, topical or oral doxepin, and topical naltrexone. B
In patients with an identified cause, treat the underlying condition. C

For chronic pruritus of unknown origin (CPUO), serlopitant, a neurokinin 1 receptor (NK1R) antagonist, was found to be more effective than placebo in reducing severity of pruritus in an RCT involving 257 adult participants with severe chronic pruritus, 55% of whom had CPUO. B

background.definition: Pruritus is defined as an irritating sensation in the upper surface of the skin usually caused by mild stimulation of pain receptors.

list.listitem: Generalized pruritus reported in up to 50% of patients with polycythemia vera, 30% of patients with Hodgkin’s lymphoma, and up to 85% of patients receiving dialysis.
In one study, xerosis was a complaint in 17% of patients with HIV.
See table for differential diagnosis.

Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) new research suggests that the epidermis itself along with the slow-conducting C neuron receptors serve as an itch receptor. This is sensitive to circulating factors such as histamine, opioids, substance P, cytokines, prostaglandins, and various ATP channels.
A reasonable initial diagnostic panel for persistent unexplained pruritus includes TSH, CBC, glucose, serum creatinine, hepatitis serology, and HIV testing. C
Further diagnostic testing is indicated based on clinical suspicion of secondary causes. C

History is the most important factor: the drug history and exposure to new creams, lotions, detergents may alert you to an underlying allergic or neurogenic cause. Also ask about risk factors for HIV and viral hepatitis.

A history of weight loss, fevers, or night sweats may suggest undiagnosed lymphoma; cold or heat intolerance along with increased weight and menstrual changes suggests thyroid disorder; nausea or anorexia may suggest renal failure; and polyuria and polydipsia suggest diabetes mellitus.

A variety of malignancies can be associated with generalized pruritus without rash, including gastrointestinal, neuroendocrine tumors, lung cancer, colorectal cancer, and breast cancer. It is especially common in hematological cancers.
Anxiety disorders can also cause psychogenic pruritus ("neurodermatitis").
Spinal cord and brain tumors are a rare cause of pruritus and should be considered during the history and physical.

Patient-reported outcome measures in pruritus with best outcome measures for reliability and validity were itch severity scale, itchy quality of life, numerical rating scales-6 and -11, visual analog scales and verbal numerical rating scale-4.

Diagnostic testing should be guided by clinical suspicion of secondary causes such as lymphoma, multiple myeloma, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism, HIV disease, renal failure, hepatitis, and polycythemia vera.

The British Academy of Dermatology guidelines (2018) recommend CBC with differential and serum ferritin in all patients with chronic generalized pruritus without rash (GPWOR). If iron overload is detected, obtain liver function tests. Other recommended tests depend on the history and clinical examination and include the above list of tests. Test for JAK2 V617F mutation in patients with suspicion of polycythemia vera due to elevated hemoglobin or hematocrit.

The European S2K guidelines (2019) recommend the following for the initial laboratory evaluation of the patient with chronic pruritus: Differential blood cell count, ESR, CRP, serum creatinine, BUN, AST/ALT/GGT, alkaline phosphatase, LDH, TSH, blucose, ferritin, and in persons over 40 year stool for occult blood.

If initial testing is not diagnostic, European S2K guidelines recommend that further testing should include: immunoelectrophoresis, hepatitis serology, cholesterol, triglycerides, calcium, parathyroidhormone, biopsy with DIF (mastocytosis, pemphigoid, etc.), a swab for candida if mucocutaneous pruritus, urine for mast cell metabolites, and further imaging studies and bone marrow investigation for mastocytosis.
Consider skin biopsy if the diagnosis remains in question.
Keep cool, use emollients, and take short tepid showers. Avoid soaking and use moisturizing soaps as opposed to antibacterial soaps. C
Begin with an H1-receptor blocker such as diphenhydramine (sedating but inexpensive) or cetirizine (less sedating but more expensive). B
Adjuncts to an H1 blocker include an H2-receptor antagonist and possibly montelukast. B
Other effective treatments include topical naltrexone and topical doxepin 5% or oral doxepin. B

For chronic pruritus of unknown origin (CPUO) serlopitant, a neurokinin 1 receptor (NK1R) antagonist, was found to be more effective than placebo in reducing severity of pruritus in an RCT involving 257 adult participants with severe chronic pruritus, 55% of whom had CPUO. B

Antihistamines (H1-receptor blockers) are usually recommended; 55% of patients with urticaria respond to H1-receptor blockade alone. Nonsedating H1-receptor blockers such as cetirizine, desloratadine, and fexofenadine are also effective. A comparison of cetirizine 10 mg versus hydroxyzine 25 mg tid found that they were similarly effective.

European S2K guidelines (2019) also recommend topical corticosteroids as initial therapy. For second or third line theapy the guidelines recommend topical calcineurin inhibitors, cannabinoid agonists, or capsaicin. Systemic therapy options include gabapentin or pregabalin, the antidepressants doxepin, mirtazapine, or paroxetine, UV phototherapy, naltrexone, and cyclosporine.

H2-receptor blockers have also been shown to be effective in small studies as a single agent, although are less effective than H1 blockers. The combination of H1-and H2-receptor blockers is more effective than H1-receptor blockers alone, and should be considered if H1-receptor blockers alone are ineffective. Another possible adjunct if H1-receptor blockers alone are not effective is montelukast. The combination of desloratadine and montelukast was more effective than desloratadine alone in one study but not in another.

Tricyclic antidepressants with H1- and H2-receptors antagonist activity (such as doxepin) have also been shown to benefit patients with urticaria. A study of topical doxepin 5% found that it was also effective for pruritus in patients with eczematous dermatitis.

Low-certainty evidence from a Cochrane review of interventions for chronic pruritus of unknown origin (CPUO) found serlopitant, a neurokinin 1 receptor (NK1R) antagonist, to be more effective than placebo in reducing severity of pruritus. The review only evaluated 1 RCT involving 257 adult participants with severe chronic pruritus, 55% of whom had CPUO.
Methotrexate has been studied in two small RCTs and was not effective as add-on therapy for patients with chronic pruritus.

listitem.strong: Treatment of pruritus associated with specific conditions

list.listitem: See also separate chapters for management of each condition
Topical naltrexone has shown promising results in patients with severe pruritus related to atopic dermatitis.
The topical JAK inhibitor ruxolitinib was effective for pruritus caused by atopic dermatitis in a small RCT (NNT = 3).

Nemolizumab is humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-31 receptor A that is given as a subcutaneous injection. An RCT with 215 patients found that it was effective for pruritus caused by atopic dermatitis (NNT = 3-6 depending on outcome).
Serlopitant once-daily was somewhat effective in an RCT of patients with pruritus due to psoriasis (NNT = 10).

In an industry-sponsored RCT enrolling 128 patients with treatment-refractory prurigo nodularis (PN), oral serlopitant 5mg daily was more effective than placebo at 4 and 8 weeks in reducing pruritus. While serlopitant received "Breakthrough Therapy" designation from the FDA in 2019 to treat PN-associated pruritus, it has not yet been granted full FDA approval.

Rifampicin is recommended by British Academy of Dermatology guidelines as first-line therapy based on good evidence. Based on lower quality evidence, cholestyramine is recommended as second line therapy, sertraline as third line therapy, and naltrexone or malmefene as fourth-line therapy. Other treatment options include systemic donabinol, phenobaritone, propofol, and topical tacrolimus ointment based only on case reports and expert opinion.
A systematic review of rifampin identified 5 randomized crossover studies with 61 patients and showed a large benefit (77% vs 20% response, p = 0.001, NNT = 2).

Similarly, for cholestatic pruritus (CP), a Cochrane review showed rifampin to be effective (mean difference [MD] of -24.6 on Visual Analogue Scale [VAS] 0 to 100, 95% CI -31.1 to -18.2), based on low quality evidence from 2 RCTs involving 42 patients. Naltrexone also appears effective (MD -2.26 on VAS 0 to 10, 95% CI -3.19 to -1.33), based on moderate quality evidence from 2 RCTs enrolling 52 participants. However, for palliative care patients with CP requiring significant doses of opioids, naltrexone may not be appropriate as it may reduce pain control.
Ondansetron and granisetron have been shown in older small studies to beneficial, but two recent RCTs found no benefit to ondansetron in patients with pruritus due to cholestasis.

A systematic review identified 42 mostly small studies of medicatl theapies for cholestatic pruritis. Cholestyramine had only been evaluated in 6 studies with 56 patients, with evidence of benefit seen in only 3 studies.

For pruritus in hemodialysis patients, a systematic review of 7 studies (largely observational or open label) with 179 patients concluded that gabapentin was effective, although adverse effects were common. The poor quality of the studies, failure to mask, and subjective nature of the outcome make a placebo effect highly likely.

Based on a Cochrane review, gabapentin is more effective than placebo for uremic pruritus (UP), with a MD of -5.9 on VAS 0 to 10 (95% CI -6.9 to -5.0), based on moderate quality evidence from 2 RCTs involving 118 patients. Nalfurafine, a K-opioid receptor agonist, based on moderate quality evidence from 3 RCTs enrolling 422 patients with UP, improves pruritus by MD of -0.95 (95% CI -1.32 to -0.58). Similarly, cromolyn sodium may be effective for UP, with MD of -2.94 points (95% CI -4.04 to -1.83), based on moderate quality evidence from 2 RCTs with a total of 100 participants.

For generalized pruritus associated with lymphoma, treatment options include cimetidine, gabapentin, carbamazepine, mirtazapine, or phototherapy based on expert opinion from the British Academy of Dermatology (BAD) guidelines. In patients with incurable lymphoma, corticosteroids may be helpful.

For generalized pruritus associated with polycythemia vera, BAD guidelines recommend cytoreductive therapy, aspirin, interferon alpha, SSRIs, PUVA, UVB phototherapy, cimetidine, or atenelol, based largely on expert opinion and case reports.
Early treatment of polycythemia vera-associated aquagenic pruritus using janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors appears to improve pruritus outcomes.

Chronic spontaneous urticaria: Two trials randomized 925 patients with chronic spontaneous urticaria to remibrutinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, or placebo. After 3 months more patients in the remibrutinib group UAS7 itch score of 6 or lower (48% vs 22%, p < .001, NNT = 4).
Opioid induced pruritus: Naltrexone is the first line therapy. Ondansetron, droperidol, mirtazapine, and gabapentin are alternatives with lower quality evidence supporting their use.
Postoperative generalized pruritus: diclofenac rectally is an option (poor quality evidence). Consider also sensitivity to detergents in sheets.
Chloroquine-induced pruritus: BAD guidelines recommend prednisolone 10 mg, niacin 50 mg, or a combination. Another option is dapsone. All of these recommendations are based on poor quality evidence.
Adult palliative care patients with pruritus: paroxetine may reduce pruritus (MD -0.78 on VAS 0 to 10; 95% CI -1.19 to -0.37), based on moderate quality evidence from a small RCT of 48 patients.
HIV-associated pruritus: hydroxyzine, pentoxifylline, triamcinolone, and indomethacin have unclear benefits in reducing pruritus, based on low quality evidence from a Cochrane review.
Generalized pruritus in pregnancy (not caused by skin lesions or systemic disease): no evidence from RCTs according to a Cochrane review.

General measures traditionally recommended but without clinical trial evidence include: keeping cool; using emollients (is evidence in atopic dermatitis); short, tepid showers, avoiding soaking, and using moisturizing soaps as opposed to antibacterial soaps.

Other measures include avoiding dry climate, sauna, alcohol based compresses, frequent bathing, and other things that can dry the skin. Also avoid contact with fragrances, preservatives, and other potential irritants.
In uremia, ultraviolet B therapy may be effective.

Patients with psychogenic pruritus may benefit from referral to a psychologist or psychiatrist. Approaches include a careful history for abuse, apparent triggers, and treatment focused on relaxation techniques, cognitive behavioral therapy, and behavioral modification.

A randomized controlled trial investigated habit reversal treatment protocol to reduce scratching in children with atopic dermatitis. This study looked at 39 children (median age 8 years) with baseline evaluation of SCORAD index and then randomised to receive habit reversal training or usual care. Mild or very severe eczema were excluded. At first visit observation of scratching patterns and situations provoking itching and scratching were noted. At 2nd visit all patients were treated with topical mometasone once daily for 3 weeks. The intervention group also had training in habit reversal repeated in next 3 visits. Assessment at 8 weeks after final visit showed both groups had improvements in SCORAD with larger improvement in intervention group (32 point vs 20 point; p <0.001).
Device-based physical therapies (ie, phototherapy, laser, electrical neurostimulation, acupuncture, cryotherapy, cold atmospheric plasma) have uncertain efficacy and safety for chronic pruritus.

Patients with pruritus have an increased 1 year risk of being diagnosed with hematologic malignancies including Hodgkin lymphoma (RR 4.4), multiple myeloma (RR 2.4), non-Hodgkin lymphoma (RR 2.4), monoclonal gammopathy (RR 1.9), myelodysplastic syndrome (RR 1.7), and lymphocytic leukemia (RR 1.5).B
